title: Peaks in Array
statement:
Call an element of an array a *peak* when it is strictly greater than both the element right before it and the element right after it. The first and last elements of an array, or of a subarray, have only one neighbour, so they are never peaks.

You get an integer array `nums` and a list `queries`. Handle the queries in order:

- `[1, l, r]`: count the peaks of the subarray `nums[l..r]` (both ends included), judging each of its elements only by neighbours that lie inside that subarray.
- `[2, index, val]`: set `nums[index]` to `val`.

Return a list holding the count of every type-1 query, in the order those queries appear.
constraints: A type-1 query [1, l, r] has 0 <= l <= r <= nums.length - 1
A type-2 query [2, index, val] has 0 <= index <= nums.length - 1 and 1 <= val <= 10^5
notes:
## Intuition

Whether index `i` is a peak depends only on `nums[i - 1]`, `nums[i]` and `nums[i + 1]`, so give every index a 0/1 flag. In a range `[l, r]`, the indices strictly inside have both neighbours in the range, so their flags hold there, and the two ends never count. A count query is the sum of the flags at `l + 1 … r - 1`, and an update changes at most the flags at `index - 1`, `index` and `index + 1`.

Recounting every range (the brute force) costs O(n) per query. A **Fenwick tree** (binary indexed tree) does point changes and prefix sums in O(log n) each.

## Approach

1. Set `peak[i]` for every inner index with `isPeak` and `add` it to the Fenwick `tree`.
2. `countBefore(i)` sums the flags of indices `0 … i - 1`.
3. For `[1, left, right]`: a range with `right - left < 2` has no inner index, so its count is 0; otherwise it is `countBefore(right) - countBefore(left + 1)`.
4. For `[2, index, value]`: write the value, recompute the flags of the neighbours `index - 1 … index + 1` that lie between 1 and `n - 2`, and `add` each flag's change.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 1, 4, 2, 5]` has one peak, index 2, so `peak = [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]`. The update `[2, 3, 4]` gives `[3, 1, 4, 4, 5]`. Rechecking indices 2 and 3, index 2 no longer beats its right neighbour, so its flag drops to 0 and `add(2, -1)` runs. The query `[1, 0, 4]` returns `countBefore(4) - countBefore(1) = 0`, so the answer is `[0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((n + q) log n): n additions build the tree and each query does a few tree operations.
- Space: O(n) for `tree` and `peak`.

## Pitfalls

- The ends of the queried range never count, even when they are peaks of the whole array.
- An update can create or destroy a peak at either neighbour, not just at `index`.
- With `left === right` the prefix difference can be -1, so short ranges return 0 directly.
- Equal neighbours, as in `[1, 3, 3, 1]`, make no peak: compare strictly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `peak[i]` | 1 when index `i` is currently a peak of the whole array |
| `tree` | the Fenwick tree over `peak`, 1-based |
| `add(i, delta)` | changes the flag sum at index `i` by `delta` |
| `countBefore(i)` | the number of peaks among indices `0 … i - 1` |
| `left`, `right` | the range of a count query |
| `index`, `value` | the position and new value of an update |
| `flag` | a neighbour's recomputed peak flag |
| `answer` | the counts collected so far |
